verificationNote: NIST entries verified against NIST IR 8547 ipd (November 2024) Tables 2-7, FIPS 186-5 (2023-02-03), SP 800-131A Rev 2 (2019-03), SP 800-38A and SP 800-38D, plus the NIST PQC project page. CNSA 2.0 entries remain needs-check — nsa.gov and media.defense.gov return HTTP 403 to automated fetches and must be checked by hand. See README.md.

IR8547.title: Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards
IR8547.status: INITIAL PUBLIC DRAFT — comment period closed 2025-01-10, not yet final as of 2026-08-01

criticalCaveat: NIST IR 8547 is an INITIAL PUBLIC DRAFT. Its dates are NIST's stated intent, not binding final guidance. Any customer-facing use MUST say 'draft guidance' — presenting draft dates as final is the exact error that loses a technically literate buyer.

definitions.deprecated: The algorithm and key length/strength may be used, but there is some security risk. The data owner must examine this risk potential and decide whether to continue use. [IR8547 §4, quoting SP 800-131A]
definitions.disallowed: The algorithm, key length/strength, parameter set, or scheme is no longer allowed for the stated purpose. [IR8547 §4]
definitions.legacyUse: May only be used to process already-protected information (e.g. decrypt existing ciphertext, verify an existing signature). [IR8547 §4]

deadlineTypesNote: Machine-readable semantics for every value `algorithms[].deadlines[].type` may take. The mapping engine (lib/mappings) reads this instead of hardcoding the vocabulary, so adding a new deadline type to this file is a data change, not a code change. `effect` drives the compliance bucket: 'prohibition' means the use named in `appliesTo` is not allowed once the deadline is in effect; 'caution' means allowed but with stated risk; 'permitted' means explicitly allowed. A deadline with `since`, or with no date at all, is IN EFFECT NOW; one with `after`/`in` is scheduled until that year passes.

deprecated.label: Deprecated
deprecated.definition: The algorithm and key length/strength may be used, but there is some security risk. The data owner must examine this risk potential and decide whether to continue use. [IR8547 §4, quoting SP 800-131A]

disallowed.label: Disallowed
disallowed.definition: The algorithm, key length/strength, parameter set, or scheme is no longer allowed for the stated purpose. [IR8547 §4]

not-approved.label: Not approved
not-approved.definition: The algorithm was withdrawn from the standard for the stated purpose and is no longer an approved choice for it.

never-approved.label: Never approved
never-approved.definition: The algorithm was never an approved choice for the stated purpose, so no transition schedule exists and none should be cited.

legacy-use.label: Legacy use permitted
legacy-use.definition: May only be used to process already-protected information (e.g. decrypt existing ciphertext, verify an existing signature). [IR8547 §4]

acceptable.label: Acceptable
acceptable.definition: Explicitly allowed by the cited standard for the use named in `appliesTo`. Reporting this use as a violation would be a false compliance claim.

detectionConfidenceNote: `detectionConfidence` qualifies a finding whose compliance answer depends on call-site context the collector cannot see. `multiplier` scales the collector's own confidence (see RawObservation.confidence); `reviewRequired` marks the finding as needing human classification before it is presented as a failure. Present only on entries where the standard's rule is use-dependent — see open gaps G-07 (DSA) and G-08 (SHA-1).

replacements.note: Only approved post-quantum key-establishment scheme at present [IR8547 §4.1.2]. Hybrid (classical + ML-KEM) is a common transitional deployment.

deadlines.note: IMPORTANT: larger RSA keys do NOT buy extra time. RSA-3072 and above are disallowed after 2035 on the same schedule.

algorithms.explanation: RSA security rests on integer factorisation, which Shor's algorithm solves in polynomial time on a cryptographically-relevant quantum computer.

replacements.note: Conservative hash-based alternative; larger signatures. Preferred where signature size is not constrained and long validity is required.

deadlines.note: P-256 and above are all disallowed after 2035. Curve size does not extend the deadline.

algorithms.explanation: ECDSA rests on the elliptic-curve discrete logarithm problem, broken by Shor's algorithm.

EdDSA (Ed25519, Ed448) is elliptic-curve based and broken by Shor's algorithm. Listed explicitly in IR 8547 Table 2, and approved by FIPS 186-5 — so unlike DSA it is still being deployed in new systems.

deadlines.source: IR8547 Table 4 (Finite Field DH and MQV; Elliptic Curve DH and MQV)

algorithms.explanation: Diffie-Hellman key agreement is broken by Shor's algorithm. This is the primary harvest-now-decrypt-later exposure: recorded sessions can be decrypted retroactively once the key exchange is broken.
algorithms.hndlSourceQuote: IR8547 §4.1.2: 'in order to mitigate the risk of "harvest now, decrypt later" attacks on network communications, application-specific guidance ... may require or recommend migration to quantum-resistant key establishment schemes before the classical schemes are generally disallowed.' — i.e. the 2035 date is a ceiling, not a target, for anything carrying long-lived secrets.

deadlines.appliesTo: verification of signatures generated prior to the implementation date of FIPS 186-5

algorithms.sourceQuote: FIPS 186-5 Appendix E: 'DSA is no longer approved for digital signature generation. DSA may be used to verify signatures generated prior to the implementation date of this standard.' and 'The specifications and algorithms for DSA are no longer included in FIPS 186-5. They may be found in FIPS 186-4.'
algorithms.explanation: DSA rests on the discrete logarithm problem and is broken by Shor's algorithm. But the important finding is not quantum: DSA has been UNAPPROVED for signature generation since FIPS 186-5 (2023-02-03), independent of any quantum timeline.
algorithms.reportingNote: REPORT DIFFERENTLY FROM RSA/ECDSA. DSA is not a 2030/2035 problem — a DSA signature-generation site is non-compliant with FIPS 186-5 TODAY. It should surface as an immediate finding with no deadline runway, not as a future PQC migration item. DSA correctly appears in no IR 8547 transition table because it was already removed from the standard.
algorithms.detectionNuance: Signature generation vs verification matters. Verification of pre-2023 signatures is permitted legacy use. The current regex cannot distinguish the two, so DSA findings should carry reduced confidence pending manual review.

detectionConfidence.reason: A pattern match cannot tell signature GENERATION (not approved since 2023-02-03) from VERIFICATION of a pre-2023 signature (permitted legacy use). Confirm which this call site does before treating it as a failure.

deadlines.source: MD5 is absent from the list of approved hash functions

algorithms.CORRECTION: Earlier versions of this file cited NIST SP 800-131A Rev 2 for MD5. That citation is WRONG — MD5 appears ZERO times in SP 800-131A Rev 2 (verified by full-text search of the PDF, 2026-08-01). MD5 has never been a NIST-approved hash function, so it does not appear in a transition document; there is nothing to transition from. The correct framing is 'not approved', not 'deprecated'.
algorithms.explanation: MD5 is classically broken by collision attacks and was never NIST-approved. Not a quantum issue.
algorithms.reportingNote: MUST NOT count toward the post-quantum risk score. Classical hygiene finding — track in a separate panel so PQC metrics are not inflated. Do not cite a transition deadline; there is none.

algorithms.quantumAttack: Grover (quadratic preimage speedup, not a break)

deadlines.appliesTo: digital signature GENERATION (except where specifically allowed by NIST protocol-specific guidance)
digital signature VERIFICATION of already-generated signatures
non-digital-signature applications that do not require collision resistance

algorithms.sourceQuote: SP 800-131A Rev 2 §9: 'SHA-1 may only be used for digital signature generation where specifically allowed by NIST protocol-specific guidance. For all other applications, SHA-1 is disallowed for digital signature generation.' / 'When used for digital signature verification, SHA-1 is allowed for legacy use.' / 'For non-digital-signature applications, the use of SHA-1 is acceptable for applications that do not require collision resistance.'
algorithms.explanation: SHA-1 is classically broken for collision resistance. IR 8547 Table 7 places it at 80 bits collision security (category <1) and 160 bits preimage security (category 1). The quantum impact on hashes is a parameter concern, not a break.
algorithms.reportingNote: Classical hygiene finding. Track separately from PQC risk.
algorithms.detectionNuance: CRITICAL: NIST's rule is USE-DEPENDENT, not algorithm-dependent. SHA-1 inside HMAC-SHA1 does not require collision resistance and is therefore ACCEPTABLE per SP 800-131A Rev 2. A blanket 'SHA-1 = alert' finding is incorrect and will be challenged. The current regex cannot tell a signature use from an HMAC use, so SHA-1 findings must carry reduced confidence and say which uses are actually disallowed. See open gap G-08.

detectionConfidence.reason: SP 800-131A Rev 2 §9 gives three different answers depending on how SHA-1 is used, and a pattern match sees none of that context. Signature generation is disallowed; signature verification is legacy use; a non-signature use that does not need collision resistance (HMAC-SHA1, for example) is acceptable. Confirm the use before treating it as a failure.

citation.document: NIST SP 800-38A (defines ECB); NIST SP 800-38D (defines GCM, the recommended replacement)

algorithms.CORRECTION: Earlier versions of this file cited SP 800-38D as the authority for AES-ECB. That is WRONG on two counts, both verified by full-text search on 2026-08-01: (1) 'ECB' appears ZERO times in SP 800-38D, which is the Galois/Counter Mode specification (November 2007); (2) ECB is defined in SP 800-38A as one of five APPROVED confidentiality modes. Saying AES-ECB 'violates SP 800-38D' would be a false compliance claim.
algorithms.complianceStatus: ECB is an APPROVED NIST confidentiality mode (SP 800-38A). Using it is not a standards violation.

bestPractice.requirement: Replace ECB with a mode that provides semantic security — AES-GCM (SP 800-38D) is the recommended authenticated choice.
bestPractice.basis: Cryptographic best practice. NOT a NIST compliance requirement — SP 800-38A lists ECB among the approved confidentiality modes, so no standard is being violated.

citation.document: NIST SP 800-38A, Recommendation for Block Cipher Modes of Operation

algorithms.explanation: ECB mode does not provide semantic security — identical plaintext blocks produce identical ciphertext, leaking structure. This is a well-established cryptographic weakness, but it is a best-practice concern, not a NIST compliance failure, and it is unrelated to quantum computing.
algorithms.reportingNote: Classical hygiene finding, and specifically a BEST-PRACTICE finding rather than a compliance finding. Do not present it as a NIST violation — an auditor will check. Track separately from PQC risk.

algorithms.explanation: IR 8547 §4.1.3: NIST's symmetric standards are 'significantly less vulnerable to known quantum attacks than the public-key cryptography standards', and all approved symmetric primitives providing at least 128 bits of classical security are believed to meet at least Category 1. Table 6: AES-128 = 128 bits / Category 1, AES-192 = 192 bits / Category 3, AES-256 = 256 bits / Category 5.
algorithms.reportingNote: DO NOT flag AES-128 as quantum-critical. NIST places it at security Category 1, i.e. adequate. Flagging it inflates the risk score and a knowledgeable buyer will notice. Note separately that CNSA 2.0 requires AES-256 for US national security systems — that is an NSS-specific requirement, not a general NIST one.
algorithms.symmetricNote: NIST has a few symmetric standards at the 112-bit security level (e.g. three-key TDEA) which IR 8547 §4.1.3 says will be disallowed in 2030.

pqcAlgorithms.note: IR 8547 §4.1.2: ML-KEM is the ONLY approved post-quantum key-establishment scheme at present.
pqcAlgorithms.sourceErratum: IR 8547 ipd Table 5 mislabels the 192- and 256-bit rows as 'ML-DSA-768' and 'ML-DSA-1024'. These are typographical errors in the draft; the correct names are ML-KEM-768 and ML-KEM-1024.

pqcAlgorithms.note: Stateless hash-based. Conservative security assumptions, large signatures. Suited to firmware/code signing with long validity.
Stateful hash-based signatures. IR 8547 Table 3 lists these as post-quantum signature options at 192 and 256 bits. Stateful — key management is unforgiving; suited to firmware signing.
Stateful hash-based signatures, listed in IR 8547 Table 3 at 192 and 256 bits.

pqcAlgorithms.status: NOT YET PUBLISHED — selected for ongoing standardization, process underway
pqcAlgorithms.warning: DO NOT cite 'FIPS 206' as an existing standard. As of 2026-08-01 the NIST PQC project page describes Falcon as selected for ongoing standardization with the process underway; no published FIPS number was confirmed. Verify before any customer-facing reference.

pqcAlgorithms.status: Selected in the 4th round; standardization underway, not yet published
pqcAlgorithms.note: Backup KEM with different mathematical assumptions to ML-KEM. IR 8547 §4.1.2 notes NIST expects to select one or more alternatives to ML-KEM in future.

citation.document: NIST PQC project page; IR 8547 ipd §4.1.2

securityStrengthBands._comment: Maps a stated parameter size to the security-strength band IR 8547 keys its transition rules on. `securityStrength` values here MUST match the strings used in each deadline's `securityStrength` field, because the engine joins on them. `assumedWhenUndetermined` marks the band assumed when a collector could not determine a key size (G-05): the conservative choice is the band with the EARLIER deadline, so an undetermined key is never reported as having more runway than it might have.
securityStrengthBands.source: NIST IR 8547 Table 2 (signatures) and Table 4 (key establishment)
